Reading the Site"},{"line":16,"text":""},{"line":17,"text":"The defining fact is the **18 m fall over 100 m up-slope** \u2014 an average grade of ~18%,"},{"line":18,"text":"with local variation likely steeper. This is not a site that can be \"flattened\"; it is a"},{"line":19,"text":"site that must be **stepped**. Three consequences drive everything else:"},{"line":20,"text":""},{"line":21,"text":"1. **Earthworks are the dominant cost and risk.** Cut-and-fill to create a single level"},{"line":22,"text":"   platform would require enormous cut at the uphill edge and enormous fill at the"},{"line":23,"text":"   downhill edge, with a high retaining structure and a large unstable fill mass. I reject"},{"line":24,"text":"   a single-platform solution."},{"line":25,"text":"2. **Water runs downhill and will run toward the building.** Surface-water management is"},{"line":26,"text":"   not an add-on; it is a primary design driver."},{"line":27,"text":"3. **Access gradients are constrained.** A continuous 18% route is at/over the practical"},{"line":28,"text":"   limit for accessible pedestrian ramps and is steep for vehicles. Circulation must be"},{"line":29,"text":"   broken into stepped, gentler segments."},{"line":30,"text":""},{"line":31,"text":"### 1.1 Approach to terrain \u2014 \"terrace and bridge, don't flatten\""},{"line":32,"text":""},{"line":33,"text":"My approach is **terrace the building into the slope** and use the natural fall as an"},{"line":34,"text":"organising device rather than fighting it:"},{"line":35,"text":""},{"line":36,"text":"- **Step the building down the slope in 3\u20134 terraces**, each terrace a level floor plate"},{"line":37,"text":"  of roughly 4\u20136 m fall. This keeps cut and fill roughly balanced *locally* at each"},{"line":38,"text":"  terrace, minimising imported fill and exported spoil."},{"line":39,"text":"- **Cut-and-fill balance per terrace** is the target: cut into the uphill side of each"},{"line":40,"text":"  terrace, use that material to build up the downhill side, so net haulage across the site"},{"line":41,"text":"  is small. Any surplus spoil is stockpiled for landscaping/berms, not exported if"},{"line":42,"text":"  avoidable."},{"line":43,"text":"- **Retaining walls** at each terrace edge. Working assumption: reinforced-concrete"},{"line":44,"text":"  cantilever or counterfort walls for the taller steps (up to ~5\u20136 m), with"},{"line":45,"text":"  **soil-nailed or anchored** solutions where the wall must also stabilise the slope"},{"line":46,"text":"  behind it. Wall type is to be confirmed by geotechnical investigation."},{"line":47,"text":"- **Drainage-first design:** an interception drain (cut-off drain) *above* the uphill edge"},{"line":48,"text":"  of the works to divert upslope catchment away from the building; a network of"},{"line":49,"text":"  surface-water channels and a below-ground drainage blanket behind every retaining wall"},{"line":50,"text":"  to relieve hydrostatic pressure; and a positive gravity outfall to the low edge of the"},{"line":51,"text":"  site. No water is allowed to pond against a wall or sit under a floor slab."},{"line":52,"text":"- **Slope stability:** the geotechnical brief must establish the existing factor of"},{"line":53,"text":"  safety, the effect of cutting the toe and loading the terraces, and whether ground"},{"line":54,"text":"  improvement, anchoring or piling is needed. I assume **no construction starts before a"},{"line":55,"text":"  slope-stability assessment** is complete."},{"line":56,"text":""},{"line":57,"text":"### 1.2 Access and circulation"},{"line":58,"text":""},{"line":59,"text":"- **Vehicles:** a one-way loop or a single access road climbing the slope at a controlled"},{"line":60,"text":"  gradient, entering at the low edge and serving each terrace level. Service/delivery"},{"line":61,"text":"  access to the cafeteria is at the lowest terrace to keep heavy vehicles off the steep"},{"line":62,"text":"  upper ramps."},{"line":63,"text":"- **Pedestrians:** the primary vertical movement is by **stepped terraces and stairs**,"},{"line":64,"text":"  with **lifts** connecting all levels. An accessible route is provided as a series of"},{"line":65,"text":"  ramps at compliant gradients (broken into landings) or, where the fall is too great, by"},{"line":66,"text":"  lift. I do **not** rely on a single long ramp at 18%."},{"line":67,"text":"- **Parking** is placed at the low (downhill) edge where the ground is closest to level,"},{"line":68,"text":"  minimising cut/fill and keeping the steep upper terraces for building and quiet uses."},{"line":69,"text":""},{"line":70,"text":"---"},{"line":71,"text":""},{"line":72,"text":"## 2. Zoning / Footprint Concept"},{"line":73,"text":""},{"line":74,"text":"The building is conceived as a **stepped spine** running up-slope, with the noisiest and"},{"line":75,"text":"most public functions at the bottom and the quietest at the top."},{"line":76,"text":""},{"line":77,"text":"| Terrace | Level (relative) | Function | Rationale |"},{"line":78,"text":"|---|---|---|---|"},{"line":79,"text":"| T1 (low edge) | \u00b10 m | **Cafeteria/canteen**, service yard, deliveries, parking | Heaviest servicing, most public, easiest vehicle access, best daylight and views; keeps food deliveries off steep ramps. |"},{"line":80,"text":"| T2 | ~ -4 to -5 m | **Lecture halls / large classrooms**, main student concourse, main entrance from mid-slope | High-traffic teaching near the main pedestrian arrival; large-span halls suit a terrace with a deep cut behind. |"},{"line":81,"text":"| T3 | ~ -9 to -10 m | **Classrooms, seminar rooms, teaching labs** | Mid-slope, quieter, flexible room sizes. |"},{"line":82,"text":"| T4 (high edge) | ~ -14 to -18 m | **Staff offices, administration, library/study** | Quietest, best views, least public traffic; offices benefit from the stable cut side. |"},{"line":83,"text":""},{"line":84,"text":"**Footprint logic:**"},{"line":85,"text":"- Building footprint is **narrow in the up-slope direction** (so each terrace is a shallow"},{"line":86,"text":"  cut/fill band) and **long across-slope** (using the 80 m width). The other five faculties are surveying"},{"line":11,"text":"their own sites in parallel; nothing here assumes shared infrastructure,"},{"line":12,"text":"shared plant, or a common material palette. Where a decision is genuinely mine"},{"line":13,"text":"to make, I make it and state the reasoning."},{"line":14,"text":""},{"line":15,"text":"---"},{"line":16,"text":""},{"line":17,"text":"## 1. Terrain and Site Conditions \u2014 Approach"},{"line":18,"text":""},{"line":19,"text":"### 1.1 What the given facts tell me"},{"line":20,"text":"- **Flat, level ground** removes the two biggest cost drivers in site work:"},{"line":21,"text":"  bulk cut-and-fill balancing and retaining structures. It also means"},{"line":22,"text":"  drainage must be *designed*, not inherited \u2014 a level site does not shed"},{"line":23,"text":"  water on its own."},{"line":24,"text":"- **Stratified soil suitable for shallow spread footings** is a green light for"},{"line":25,"text":"  conventional pad/strip foundations, but \"stratified\" is the operative word:"},{"line":26,"text":"  layered profiles can carry a soft or compressible band, or a perched water"},{"line":27,"text":"  table, at a depth that a shallow footing might just clip. This must be"},{"line":28,"text":"  confirmed, not assumed."},{"line":29,"text":""},{"line":30,"text":"### 1.2 Site investigation I would commission before design freeze"},{"line":31,"text":"1. **Window sampling / trial pits** (minimum 4\u20136, at the corners and centre of"},{"line":32,"text":"   the proposed footprint) to log layer boundaries, thicknesses, and the"},{"line":33,"text":"   consistency/density of each stratum."},{"line":34,"text":"2. **SPT (standard penetration test) boreholes** to at least 2\u20133\u00d7 the"},{"line":35,"text":"   anticipated footing width below formation level, to confirm the bearing"},{"line":36,"text":"   stratum is continuous under the whole footprint and not a lens."},{"line":37,"text":"3. **Groundwater monitoring** \u2014 a standpipe or two, read over a wet season if"},{"line":38,"text":"   possible \u2014 to establish the true water table and any perched horizon."},{"line":39,"text":"4. **Chemical testing** (sulphate/chloride, pH) on soil and groundwater to"},{"line":40,"text":"   select the correct cement type and concrete cover for durability."},{"line":41,"text":"5. **Plate load or hand-vane tests** where the profile is variable, to derive a"},{"line":42,"text":"   defensible allowable bearing pressure rather than a default."},{"line":43,"text":""},{"line":44,"text":"**Design assumption pending that investigation:** allowable bearing pressure of"},{"line":45,"text":"~150 kPa on the competent stratum, with footings founded *below* any soft band"},{"line":46,"text":"and above the water table. If the investigation reveals a soft layer within"},{"line":47,"text":"footing influence, the fallback is to deepen pads to the competent layer"},{"line":48,"text":"(still shallow construction) or, if that layer is too deep, a stiffened raft."},{"line":49,"text":"I would not jump to piles on a site described as suitable for shallow footings"},{"line":50,"text":"unless the investigation forces it."},{"line":51,"text":""},{"line":52,"text":"### 1.3 Site-level moves that follow from \"flat and level\""},{"line":53,"text":"- **Positive drainage design:** a minimum 1:60 fall on external paving away"},{"line":54,"text":"  from the building, perimeter land drains, and a designed attenuation/"},{"line":55,"text":"  soakaway strategy. On flat ground, a blocked gully becomes a flood."},{"line":56,"text":"- **Finished floor level** set a clear 300\u2013450 mm above surrounding external"},{"line":57,"text":"  ground to give freeboard against surface water."},{"line":58,"text":"- **Orientation:** the plot is effectively square, so orientation is a free"},{"line":59,"text":"  choice. I would set the long axis of the teaching block roughly east\u2013west so"},{"line":60,"text":"  the deep-plan lecture halls face north/south and glazing is controlled on the"},{"line":61,"text":"  east/west elevations (low sun = glare and heat gain in a lecture theatre)."},{"line":62,"text":"- **Access and servicing:** a perimeter service loop is not achievable on a"},{"line":63,"text":"  60 m square with a large footprint; I would plan a single controlled vehicle"},{"line":64,"text":"  entry with a lay-by for deliveries and refuse, kept clear of the pedestrian"},{"line":65,"text":"  route to the cafeteria."},{"line":66,"text":""},{"line":67,"text":"---"},{"line":68,"text":""},{"line":69,"text":"## 2. Rough Zoning and Footprint Concept"},{"line":70,"text":""},{"line":71,"text":"### 2.1 Massing logic"},{"line":72,"text":"A 60 m \u00d7 60 m plot with a mid-sized faculty brief points to a **compact,"},{"line":73,"text":"two-storey block** rather than a sprawling single storey: it preserves"},{"line":74,"text":"external space for circulation, planting, and drainage, and it keeps the"},{"line":75,"text":"cafeteria at ground level with a short, legible route from the main entrance."},{"line":76,"text":""},{"line":77,"text":"### 2.2 Indicative zoning (plan concept)"},{"line":78,"text":"| Zone | Location | Notes |"},{"line":79,"text":"|---|---|---|"},{"line":80,"text":"| **Entrance / reception / circulation core** | Front (south) face, centre | Single point of control; stairs + lift core; the \"spine\" everything hangs off. |"},{"line":81,"text":"| **Lecture halls & classrooms** | North and east wings, both floors | Deep-plan, minimal glazing on east/west; acoustic separation from the core. |"},{"line":82,"text":"| **Staff offices** | Upper floor, quieter west/south-west edge | Cellular offices and small meeting rooms; daylight from the quieter elevation. |"},{"line":83,"text":"| **Cafeteria / canteen** | Ground floor, south-east corner | Direct external access, own delivery door, separated from teaching circulation. |"},{"line":84,"text":"| **Kitchen / servery / stores / plant** | Behind the cafeteria, ground floor | Back-of-house adjacency to the delivery lay-by; refuse store adjacent. |"},{"line":85,"text":"| **Plant rooms / risers** | Core and roof | Centralised so services runs stay short. |"},{"line":86,"text":""},{"line":87,"text":"### 2.3 Indicative areas (order-of-magnitude, to be tested)"},{"line":88,"text":"- Lecture halls/classrooms: ~1,200\u20131,500 m\u00b2"},{"line":89,"text":"- Staff offices: ~500\u2013700 m\u00b2"},{"line":90,"text":"- Cafeteria + servery + kitchen + stores: ~450\u2013600 m\u00b2"},{"line":91,"text":"- Circulation, core, WCs, plant: ~600\u2013800 m\u00b2"},{"line":92,"text":"- **Total gross: ~2,800\u20133,600 m\u00b2 over two storeys**, i.e. a footprint of"},{"line":93,"text":"  roughly **1,400\u20131,800 m\u00b2** \u2014 comfortably inside the plot with room for"},{"line":94,"text":"  external works, drainage, and a service yard."},{"line":95,"text":""},{"line":96,"text":"### 2.4 Structural grid"},{"line":97,"text":"A regular **7.5 m \u00d7 7.5 m** column grid suits both the teaching spaces and the"},{"line":98,"text":"cafeteria, keeps beam depths economical, and lets the cafeteria span be handled"},{"line":99,"text":"by the same frame as the rest of the building. Grid regularity is the single"},{"line":100,"text":"biggest lever on construction cost and speed here."},{"line":101,"text":""},{"line":102,"text":"---"},{"l

**Status:** Final building plan (post-survey coordination)
**Site:** Flat, level plot, approx. 60 m × 60 m (~3,600 m²)
**Soil:** Stratified (layered) profile, generally suitable for standard shallow
spread-footing foundations.
**Brief:** Lecture halls/classrooms for a mid-sized faculty, staff offices, and a
cafeteria/canteen serving students and staff.

This plan finalises the footprint/zoning and the material choices for the
Faculty of Business building. It is based on my own survey (SURVEY_BUSINESS.md)
and on a full read of the five peer surveys (Engineering, Computing, Law,
Medicine, Arts). Section 7 states explicitly what a peer's survey changed in my
plan and what it did not.

---

## 1. Basis and Method

My own survey established the site as benign: flat, level ground with stratified
soil suited to shallow spread footings, subject to a confirming geotechnical
investigation. The peer surveys fall into two groups:

- **Four flat-site faculties** (Computing, Law, Medicine, Arts) surveyed plots
  materially identical to mine — flat, level, ~60 m × 60 m, stratified soil.
  Their findings are directly transferable to my site.
- **One hillside faculty** (Engineering) surveyed an ~80 m × 100 m plot with an
  ~18 m fall. Its findings are driven by slope and are not transferable to a
  level plot (see §7.4).

I read all six surveys before finalising. Where a peer's finding was relevant to
my building, I adopted it and say so below; where it was not, I say that too.

---

## 2. Site and Foundation Strategy (Finalised)

### 2.1 Terrain

Flat, level ground. No cut-and-fill balancing problem, no retaining structures,
no slope-stability risk. The design consequences are the same as those
identified by my own survey and by the other flat-site faculties:

- **Positive drainage is a design responsibility, not an inherited condition.**
  A level plot does not shed water on its own.
- **Finished floor level** set a clear 300–450 mm above surrounding external
  ground to give freeboard against surface water.
- **Orientation is a free choice** on a square plot; the long axis of the
  teaching block is set roughly east–west so deep-plan lecture halls face
  north/south and glazing is controlled on the east/west elevations.

### 2.2 Foundations (finalised)

**Primary strategy: reinforced-concrete pad (spread) footings on a graded,
compacted formation, tied by a continuous reinforced ground-beam grid.**

The ground beams are not optional detailing — they are the mechanism that
distributes load and limits differential movement where the stratified layers
vary across the 60 m × 60 m plot. All footings are founded on the same competent
stratum where feasible, and column loads are kept reasonably uniform across the
grid so that no footing is loaded out of proportion to its neighbours.

**Designated fallback: a stiffened raft/mat foundation.** If the geotechnical
investigation reveals a soft or compressible layer within the footing influence
zone that cannot be economically deepened past, the pre-agreed fallback is a
raft rather than a change of foundation type under part of the building. A raft
spreads load, tolerates the modest differential settlement that layered soils
produce, and doubles as a moisture barrier under the ground floor. Abrupt
changes of foundation type under one building are to be avoided.

**Geotechnical investigation to be commissioned before design freeze** —
boreholes/trial pits to below the anticipated influence zone, SPT/CPT, layer
logging, groundwater monitoring, and bearing-capacity derivation. The
"generally suitable" description is a starting assumption, not a substitute for
site-specific data.

### 2.3 Peer inputs adopted into the foundation and ground strategy

Three findings from peer surveys were **not** in my own survey and have been
adopted into this plan:

1. **Soil and groundwater chemical testing (from Computing).** Computing's
   survey specifies chemical testing (sulphate/chloride, pH) on soil and
   groundwater to select the correct cement type and concrete cover for
   durability. My own survey did not include this. It is directly relevant to my
   building — same stratified soil, same shallow footings, same buried concrete
   — so I have added it to my geotechnical brief. **This changed my plan.**
2. **Construction-stage dewatering and seasonal scheduling (from Medicine).**
   Medicine's survey notes that with a shallow or perched water table,
   dewatering during footing excavation may be needed, and that foundation works
   should be scheduled for the drier season where possible. My own survey
   treated the water table only as a design input, not as a construction-stage
   constraint. I have adopted this as a construction-planning requirement.
   **This changed my plan.**
3. **Raft as a moisture barrier (from Law).** Law's survey makes the point that
   a raft foundation also acts as a moisture barrier under the ground floor.
   This is a genuine additional benefit that strengthens the case for the raft
   fallback already described in §2.2, and it is now recorded as one of the
   reasons for that fallback. **This refined a decision I had already made.**

---

## 3. Footprint and Zoning (Finalised)

### 3.1 Massing

A **compact, 2–3 storey block** within the plot. A 60 m × 60 m plot with a
mid-sized faculty brief does not support a sprawling low-rise scheme: a compact
block preserves external space for circulation, drainage, service access and
amenity, and keeps the cafeteria at ground level with a short, legible route
from the main entrance. Indicative footprint ~1,400–1,800 m² (roughly 40–50% of
the plot).

### 3.2 Zoning

        NORTH (quiet / academic)

```

**Zoning principles (finalised):**

**Status:** Final building plan (post-survey coordination)
**Site:** Flat, level plot, approx. 60 m × 60 m (~3,600 m²)
**Soil:** Stratified (layered) profile, generally suitable for standard shallow
spread-footing foundations.
**Brief:** Lecture halls/classrooms for a mid-sized faculty, staff offices, and a
cafeteria/canteen serving students and staff.

This plan finalises the footprint/zoning and the material choices for the
Faculty of Business building. It is based on my own survey (SURVEY_BUSINESS.md)
and on a full read of the five peer surveys (Engineering, Computing, Law,
Medicine, Arts). Section 7 states explicitly what a peer's survey changed in my
plan and what it did not.

---

## 1. Basis and Method

My own survey established the site as benign: flat, level ground with stratified
soil suited to shallow spread footings, subject to a confirming geotechnical
investigation. The peer surveys fall into two groups:

- **Four flat-site faculties** (Computing, Law, Medicine, Arts) surveyed plots
  materially identical to mine — flat, level, ~60 m × 60 m, stratified soil.
  Their findings are directly transferable to my site.
- **One hillside faculty** (Engineering) surveyed an ~80 m × 100 m plot with an
  ~18 m fall. Its findings are driven by slope and are not transferable to a
  level plot (see §7.4).

I read all six surveys before finalising. Where a peer's finding was relevant to
my building, I adopted it and say so below; where it was not, I say that too.

---

## 2. Site and Foundation Strategy (Finalised)

### 2.1 Terrain

Flat, level ground. No cut-and-fill balancing problem, no retaining structures,
no slope-stability risk. The design consequences are the same as those
identified by my own survey and by the other flat-site faculties:

- **Positive drainage is a design responsibility, not an inherited condition.**
  A level plot does not shed water on its own.
- **Finished floor level** set a clear 300–450 mm above surrounding external
  ground to give freeboard against surface water.
- **Orientation is a free choice** on a square plot; the long axis of the
  teaching block is set roughly east–west so deep-plan lecture halls face
  north/south and glazing is controlled on the east/west elevations.

### 2.2 Foundations (finalised)

**Primary strategy: reinforced-concrete pad (spread) footings on a graded,
compacted formation, tied by a continuous reinforced ground-beam grid.**

The ground beams are not optional detailing — they are the mechanism that
distributes load and limits differential movement where the stratified layers
vary across the 60 m × 60 m plot. All footings are founded on the same competent
stratum where feasible, and column loads are kept reasonably uniform across the
grid so that no footing is loaded out of proportion to its neighbours.

**Designated fallback: a stiffened raft/mat foundation.** If the geotechnical
investigation reveals a soft or compressible layer within the footing influence
zone that cannot be economically deepened past, the pre-agreed fallback is a
raft rather than a change of foundation type under part of the building. A raft
spreads load, tolerates the modest differential settlement that layered soils
produce, and doubles as a moisture barrier under the ground floor. Abrupt
changes of foundation type under one building are to be avoided.

**Geotechnical investigation to be commissioned before design freeze** —
boreholes/trial pits to below the anticipated influence zone, SPT/CPT, layer
logging, groundwater monitoring, and bearing-capacity derivation. The
"generally suitable" description is a starting assumption, not a substitute for
site-specific data.

adopted into this plan:

1. **Soil and groundwater chemical testing (from Computing).** Computing's
   survey specifies chemical testing (sulphate/chloride, pH) on soil and
   groundwater to select the correct cement type and concrete cover for
   durability. My own survey did not include this. It is directly relevant to my
   building — same stratified soil, same shallow footings, same buried concrete
   — so I have added it to my geotechnical brief. **This changed my plan.**
2. **Construction-stage dewatering and seasonal scheduling (from Medicine).**
   Medicine's survey notes that with a shallow or perched water table,
   dewatering during footing excavation may be needed, and that foundation works
   should be scheduled for the drier season where possible. My own survey
   treated the water table only as a design input, not as a construction-stage
   constraint. I have adopted this as a construction-planning requirement.
   **This changed my plan.**
3. **Raft as a moisture barrier (from Law).** Law's survey makes the point that
   a raft foundation also acts as a moisture barrier under the ground floor.
   This is a genuine additional benefit that strengthens the case for the raft
   fallback already described in §2.2, and it is now recorded as one of the
   reasons for that fallback. **This refined a decision I had already made.**
